vignette:
The Weight of the Water

Harjit is an eighty-year-old retired Coast Guard officer who spent the better part of four decades patrolling the coastal waters of British Columbia. He is a careful man - careful in the way he folds his newspaper each morning, careful in the way he measures his words, careful in the way he still checks the weather forecast twice before leaving his small apartment in Vancouver. Carefulness, for most of his life, was a form of love. It was also, he believed, a form of protection.

Thirty-one years ago, during a night rescue operation in heavy fog off the Strait of Georgia, Harjit made a decision that he has never stopped remaking in his mind. A distress call had come in from a small fishing vessel taking on water. Visibility was near zero. He was at the helm, and he ordered a speed that his instincts told him was manageable. What he could not see - what no one could have seen - was a man in the water, a crew member who had already gone overboard from the stricken vessel. The impact was brief and catastrophic. The man survived, but lost his right arm and sustained a spinal injury that left him partially paralyzed for the rest of his life.

The official inquiry cleared Harjit of negligence. His commanding officer told him he had done everything correctly. He received a commendation the following year for a separate rescue. He kept working. He told almost no one, including his wife, Paramjit, how completely something had broken open inside him that night.

For years, he managed. He stayed busy. The sea, paradoxically, was the only place where he felt competent enough to outrun what had happened. But after he retired twelve years ago, and especially after Paramjit died four years ago, the management stopped working. Now there is nothing between him and the memory.

He wakes most nights between two and three in the morning with his heart hammering, certain he can hear the sound of the hull moving through water, certain he is back at the helm. He lies in the dark of his apartment and does not move until the feeling passes, which sometimes takes an hour. He has not slept more than four consecutive hours in longer than he can remember.

During the day, he avoids the waterfront entirely, though he spent a lifetime loving it. He takes a longer route to the grocery store so he does not have to smell the inlet. When his grandson showed him a documentary about the Coast Guard last winter, Harjit left the room without explanation and sat in the bathroom until he heard the television go quiet. He told the boy he had a headache. He is ashamed of the lie and more ashamed of the reason for it.

He describes himself as hollowed out. He says this plainly, without self-pity, in the same measured tone he uses to describe the weather. He does not feel entitled to his suffering - this is perhaps the most persistent feature of his inner life. The man in the water lost an arm. Lost the use of his legs. Harjit lost nothing he can name, and yet he cannot stop losing it.

He carries a particular contempt for himself that has deepened with age. He thinks about the injured man often, wonders whether he is still alive, has never permitted himself to find out. To look would feel, he says, like asking for something he has not earned. He keeps a photograph of Paramjit on the kitchen table and speaks to her sometimes in the mornings over his tea. He tells her he is fine. He is not fine. He knows she would have known the difference, and the knowing of that - that she is gone and cannot see through him anymore - is its own quiet grief layered beneath everything else.

He came to therapy because his daughter asked him to. He sat down in the chair, straightened his collar, and said he wasn't sure he had anything worth talking about.
